newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE - Albanian pyramid "timebombs" still tick.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Albanian pyramid "timebombs" still tick.

text.p: Kujtim Sirna isn't interested in the pyramid investment schemes that sparked Albania's ruinous riots. He barely ekes out a living hauling cement and used furniture around Tirana in a horse-drawn cart.

"I make 800 to 900 leks ($4.50 to $5) a day and I work seven days a week," said 34-year-old Sirna as he waited patiently with his horse Kuqo in the rutted, muddy street outside a central market in the capital of Europe's poorest country.
"My wife is unemployed, my sons are one and four years old, but with this and some social assistance we can live," he said.

What did he think of the investment schemes, which paid up to 200 percent interest in three months before the collapse of several of them led to the riots in March which devastated the country and brought down the government?
"It's better to keep your money at home," he said.

That's what many Albanians think after losing thousands of dollars apiece when the schemes, in which people had invested up to $1.5 billion, an amount equivalent to half of Gross Domestic Product, failed.

The riots caused widespread devastation of foreign-owned as well as Albanian businesses in this country which was just beginning to develop a free market economy after a half century of the most benighted Stalinist dictatorship in Europe.
REMAINING INVESTMENT FIRMS ON BRINK OF COLLAPSE

The international community is trying to repair the damage by prodding Albania's squabbling political parties to hold early elections on June 29. A 6,500-strong Italian-led international force provides a semblance of authority in the chaotic country.

But one thing nobody has done so far is to come to grips with the remaining investment firms, some of which, according to financial experts, are tottering on the brink and whose collapse could strip Albanians of hundreds of millions of dollars more.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) advised Albania last month that it should deal urgently with the problems of its soaring budget deficit and the pyramid schemes.
"Albania's economic problems are very serious," the IMF said. "We are particularly concerned about two issues, the budget deficit and resolution of the pyramid scheme problem."

Parliament, still dominated by President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party although the government was dissolved during the riots, passed a watered-down bill which left out a crucial bit giving control to auditors until it was determined whether a company was or was not a pyramid, diplomats said.

Pyramid schemes promise big returns on investments but usually have few or no assets. They rely on cash from new customers to pay existing clients and collapse when the number of customers at the "base" becomes so large they can't be paid.

Finance Minister Arben Malaj said Albanians were not so naive as to think the pyramids were spinning gold from straw, but were trying to cash in on what they perceived as widespread laundering of money through them.
"They didn't believe the profit came from their business activities," he told Reuters in an interview.
"They were not clear where the money was coming from but they were hoping these companies still had these 'services' and continued to play with them and did not withdraw their money."

Now the future of the remaining funds, most of which have gone to ground after being the most colourful players on the Albanian business scene, backing sports teams, sponsoring beauty contests and giving parties, is a political hot potato.

"The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank say the government must close them down but no one is anxious to take the plunge before the elections, and whoever wins will be stuck with an albatross around the neck," one Western diplomat said.
"Every macroeconomic indicator here is off the scale and when they have a crisis situation and need to rise to the occasion they show no sign of doing so," the diplomat added.
"This could end up like the Somalia of Europe. Large sections are in a state of anarchy and are run by warlords."
That's what worries businessmen, Albanian and foreign, who invested in Albania because of its proximity to Western Europe, cheap labour and mineral wealth only to have the investments trashed.
SOME INVESTORS OPTIMISTIC ABOUT FUTURE

Vebi Velija, an Albanian born in Macedonia, said losses amounted to $7.9 million when his ultra-modern cigarette manufacturing plant in the southeast of the country was ransacked and stripped from top to bottom.
The plant won't be rebuilt in the same place, and nothing will be done until after the elections, he said.
"I will rebuild it when the political situation is normalised, after the elections, and if not we cannot do anything," he told Reuters in an interview.
Another foreign businessman, who asked not to be identified, said his new warehouse in one of Albania's ports had been looted during the riots, causing $200,000 in damage.
"It was like they were taking out their anger on the stuff," he said, adding that insurance would not cover losses.
But he said the company had no intention of pulling out, because business prospects looked good for the long term.
Carlos Elbirt, the World Bank's resident representative, echoed that optimistic view, although the bank has not approved any new projects recently, pending the election.
"This country has a lot to offer," he said. "It is too poor but...it has natural resources, human resources."
"...But I know this process (the election) could go well or could go badly. I hope it will be in the right direction but there are reasons to be concerned," he said.
People who had money invested in the pyramid schemes are also worried as Albania heads to a vote with the country still awash with weapons looted during the riots.

"We hope that after the elections the situation will stabilise," said Kujtim Basha, a 52-year-old former army officer sacked without a pension when the military was cut back after communism collapsed.
Basha, who now sells cheese in the market, said he invested 150,000 leks ($15,000 at the time) in two schemes but got back from one what he lost in the other.
"I am not too angry, all this has been a test for our ignorance," he said. "But I am angry about our politicians and experts who did not warn the people."
